expectedText:
TENANT HABITABILITY REMEDIES: REPAIR-AND-DEDUCT AND RETALIATION PROTECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

TENANT'S NOTICE AND DECLARATION — HABITABILITY DEFECT, REPAIR-AND-DEDUCT, AND RETALIATION INFORMATION
I, Jordan Lee, am the tenant renting 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 from Pat Morgan ("Landlord"). On August 15, 2026, I gave Landlord notice of the following condition at the property that I believe needs repair: A persistent roof leak in the main bedroom that has caused visible mold growth.

This information sheet describes two separate provisions of California law: Civil Code section 1942, which addresses a tenant's ability, in specified circumstances, to repair a dilapidated condition and deduct the cost from rent, or to vacate the premises; and Civil Code section 1942.5, which addresses certain landlord conduct following specified tenant activity, including a notice of the kind described above. Filling in this information sheet is not itself the notice required by Civil Code section 1942, does not by itself exercise any right to repair and deduct or to vacate, does not file anything with any court or agency, and does not determine that the condition described above in fact renders 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 untenantable, that Landlord in fact neglected to repair it within a reasonable time, or that any specific conduct by Landlord was in fact retaliatory.

THE REPAIR-AND-DEDUCT (OR VACATE) REMEDY
If, within a reasonable time after written or oral notice to the landlord (or the landlord's agent) of a dilapidated condition making the premises untenantable that the landlord ought to repair, the landlord neglects to do so, the tenant may repair the condition and deduct the cost from the rent when due — so long as the cost of the repair does not require spending more than one month's rent on the premises — or the tenant may instead vacate the premises, in which case the tenant is discharged from paying further rent or performing other lease conditions as of the date of vacating. This remedy is not available to a tenant more than twice in any 12-month period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If within a reasonable time after written or oral notice to the landlord or his agent, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1962, of dilapidations rendering the premises untenantable which the landlord ought to repair, the landlord neglects to do so, the tenant may repair the same himself where the cost of such repairs does not require an expenditure more than one month’s rent of the premises and deduct the expenses of such repairs from the rent when due, or the tenant may vacate the premises, in which case the tenant shall be discharged from further payment of rent, or performance of other conditions as of the date of vacating the premises. This remedy shall not be available to the tenant more than twice in any 12-month period."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the repair-and-deduct or vacate remedy and its cost/frequency limits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.)
  Known gap: The dollar limit on this remedy is not a fixed figure — it is one month's rent, which scales with whatever the rent for the specific unit happens to be, rather than a flat statutory cap; a fixed-dollar-cap assumption for this statute would be inaccurate as applied to current text. The statute's trigger — a dilapidation "rendering the premises untenantable" — uses the same "untenantable" concept this corpus's Residential Lease Agreement document already addresses in its own habitability clauses (drawing on Civil Code §§ 1941 and 1941.1); this clause does not restate that definition and should be read together with those clauses rather than as an independent definition of untenantability. The twice-in-any-12-month-period limit stated here is specific to this repair-and-deduct/vacate remedy; a separate, differently-worded 12-month limit exists elsewhere in this document for the retaliation-protection remedy addressed in Civil Code § 1942.5, and the two should not be conflated. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; repair-and-deduct rights, where they exist, vary by state in their dollar limits, frequency limits, and notice requirements. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific condition renders a specific unit untenantable, that a specific landlord failed to repair within a reasonable time, or that a specific tenant properly exercised this remedy.

NOTICE-TIMING PRESUMPTION, TENANT-CAUSED CONDITIONS, AND CUMULATIVE REMEDIES
If a tenant acts to repair and deduct after the 30th day following notice to the landlord, the tenant is presumed to have acted after a reasonable time — a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence, and one that does not prevent a tenant from repairing and deducting after a shorter notice if the circumstances require it. The repair-and-deduct remedy described elsewhere in this document is not available if the condition was caused by the tenant's own violation of a separate statute (Civil Code §§ 1929 and 1941.2). That remedy is in addition to any other remedy available under this chapter, the rental agreement, or other applicable statutory or common law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For the purposes of this section, if a tenant acts to repair and deduct after the 30th day following notice, he is presumed to have acted after a reasonable time. The presumption established by this subdivision is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence and shall not be construed to prevent a tenant from repairing and deducting after a shorter notice if all the circumstances require shorter notice."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the 30-day reasonable-time presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.)
  "The tenant’s remedy under subdivision (a) shall not be available if the condition was caused by the violation of Section 1929 or 1941.2."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, exclusion for tenant-caused conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.)
  "The remedy provided by this section is in addition to any other remedy provided by this chapter, the rental agreement, or other applicable statutory or common law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, this remedy is cumulative with other remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.)
  Known gap: This 30-day "reasonable time" presumption is a distinct legal concept from the rebuttable-presumption-style protection this document's retaliation clauses describe under Civil Code § 1942.5 — this one is about whether a tenant waited long enough after giving notice before repairing and deducting, not about whether a landlord's later conduct toward the tenant was retaliatory; the two shouldn't be read as the same presumption. The excluding condition referenced here — a condition caused by violation of Civil Code § 1929 or § 1941.2 — is quoted from § 1942 by cross-reference only; this document does not independently fetch, verify, or describe the text of § 1929 or § 1941.2 themselves, and no claim is made here about what conduct those sections actually require of a tenant. All three citations below are subsections ((b), (c), and (d)) of the same statutory section as the remedy described in this document's companion clause, not independently authored sources; this is disclosed here rather than presented as multiple separate authorities. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific tenant's repair-and-deduct timing was reasonable, or that any specific condition falls within this exclusion.

RETALIATION PROTECTION: THE 180-DAY RULE AND THE PROTECTED TENANT CONDUCT IT COVERS
If a landlord retaliates against a tenant because the tenant exercised rights under this chapter of the Civil Code — which includes the habitability and repair-and-deduct rights addressed elsewhere in this document — or because the tenant complained to an appropriate agency about the tenantability of a dwelling, and the tenant is not in default on rent, the landlord may not recover possession of the dwelling, cause the tenant to quit involuntarily, increase the rent, or decrease any services within 180 days after any of the following: the tenant's good-faith notice given under Civil Code section 1942, notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, or oral complaint to the landlord about tenantability; the tenant's good-faith written complaint (or oral complaint that is registered or otherwise recorded in writing) to an appropriate agency, of which the landlord has notice, made for the purpose of getting a tenantability condition corrected; an inspection or citation resulting from that agency complaint, where the landlord did not have notice of the complaint itself; the filing of a judicial or arbitration proceeding involving a tenantability issue; or a judgment or arbitration award on a tenantability issue decided against the landlord. The 180-day period runs from the latest of these dates.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the lessor retaliates against the lessee because of the exercise by the lessee of the lessee’s rights under this chapter or because of the lessee’s complaint to an appropriate agency as to tenantability of a dwelling, and if the lessee of a dwelling is not in default as to the payment of rent, the lessor may not recover possession of a dwelling in any action or proceeding, cause the lessee to quit involuntarily, increase the rent, or decrease any services within 180 days of any of the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the core 180-day retaliation prohibition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "(1) After the date upon which the lessee, in good faith, has given notice pursuant to Section 1942, has provided notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, or has made an oral complaint to the lessor regarding tenantability.(2) After the date upon which the lessee, in good faith, has filed a written complaint, or an oral complaint which is registered or otherwise recorded in writing, with an appropriate agency, of which the lessor has notice, for the purpose of obtaining correction of a condition relating to tenantability.(3) After the date of an inspection or issuance of a citation, resulting from a complaint described in paragraph (2) of which the lessor did not have notice.(4) After the filing of appropriate documents commencing a judicial or arbitration proceeding involving the issue of tenantability.(5) After entry of judgment or the signing of an arbitration award, if any, when in the judicial proceeding or arbitration the issue of tenantability is determined adversely to the lessor.In each instance, the 180-day period shall run from the latest applicable date referred to in paragraphs (1) to (5), inclusive."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(a)(1)-(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the specific list of triggering tenant conduct and dates (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  Known gap: The statute's own text does not use the word "presumption" anywhere in this subsection — it is written as a direct prohibition on specified landlord conduct within the 180-day window, not as an evidentiary presumption the tenant must invoke; describing it as creating a "presumption of retaliation" is a common shorthand, but not the statute's own terminology, and this document uses the statute's own "may not" framing instead. One of the listed triggering events — the tenant's good-faith notice "pursuant to Section 1942" — is the direct textual link between this retaliation protection and the repair-and-deduct notice described in this document's other clauses; the broader "exercise ... of rights under this chapter" language in the opening sentence extends further, to the habitability rights this corpus's existing Residential Lease Agreement document separately addresses, but this document does not independently trace every right "under this chapter" beyond what the quoted text itself lists. This section separately contains a broader anti-retaliation prohibition, in subdivisions (d) and (e), covering a landlord's retaliation against a tenant for organizing or participating in a tenants' association or lawfully exercising rights generally (with the tenant bearing the burden of producing evidence of retaliation, rather than the 180-day timing rule described here) — that broader prohibition is not covered by this document's clauses. Both citations below are from the same statutory subsection, (a), not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; retaliation protections for tenants, where they exist, vary by state in their triggers, timing windows, and remedies. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord conduct was in fact retaliatory, or that any specific tenant conduct falls within the protected categories described here.

FREQUENCY LIMIT, IMMIGRATION-STATUS REPORTING, AND THE LANDLORD'S OPPORTUNITY TO SHOW A LAWFUL REASON
A tenant may not invoke the 180-day retaliation rule described elsewhere in this document more than once in any 12-month period. Reporting, or threatening to report, the tenant or individuals known to the landlord to be associated with the tenant to immigration authorities is itself a form of retaliatory conduct the statute prohibits, and that specific prohibition does not limit the broader definition of retaliatory conduct the statute otherwise covers. The statute does not limit a landlord's lawful exercise of rights under a lease, agreement, or other law, or a landlord's right to take the described actions for any lawful cause, and any waiver by a tenant of rights under this statute is void as against public policy. Despite the 180-day rule, a landlord may still recover possession, increase rent, decrease services, or take the other described actions within that period if the notice of termination, rent increase, or other act — or a pleading or statement of issues in an arbitration — states the ground on which the landlord, in good faith, is acting; if the tenant disputes that stated ground, the landlord must establish its truth at the trial or other hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A lessee may not invoke subdivision (a) more than once in any 12-month period."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the once-per-12-months limit on invoking this protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "To report, or to threaten to report, the lessee or individuals known to the landlord to be associated with the lessee to immigration authorities is a form of retaliatory conduct prohibited under subdivision (a). This subdivision shall in no way limit the definition of retaliatory conduct prohibited under this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, immigration-status reporting as retaliatory conduct (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "This section does not limit in any way the exercise by the lessor of the lessor’s rights under any lease or agreement or any law pertaining to the hiring of property or the lessor’s right to do any of the acts described in subdivision (a) or (d) for any lawful cause. Any waiver by a lessee of the lessee’s rights under this section is void as contrary to public policy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, lawful-cause carve-out and anti-waiver rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivisions (a) to (f), inclusive, a lessor may recover possession of a dwelling and do any of the other acts described in subdivision (a) within the period or periods prescribed therein, or within subdivision (d), if the notice of termination, rent increase, or other act, and any pleading or statement of issues in an arbitration, if any, states the ground upon which the lessor, in good faith, seeks to recover possession, increase rent, or do any of the other acts described in subdivision (a) or (d). If the statement is controverted, the lessor shall establish its truth at the trial or other hearing."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the landlord's stated-ground safe harbor and burden at hearing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  Known gap: This 12-month, once-per-period limit on invoking the retaliation rule is a different limit from the twice-in-any-12-month-period limit this document describes for actually exercising the repair-and-deduct remedy itself under Civil Code § 1942(a) — the two limits apply to different rights and should not be treated as the same rule. The stated-ground mechanism described in this clause is, on this statute's own text, the actual rebuttal-like structure built into this protection: rather than a labeled presumption the tenant must overcome, the statute lets a landlord act within the 180-day window if the landlord states a good-faith, non-retaliatory ground in the notice or pleading itself, with the landlord bearing the burden of proving that stated ground true if the tenant disputes it. All four citations below are subsections — (b), (c), (f), and (g) — of the same statutory section as the core prohibition described in this document's companion clause, not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord's stated ground was in fact lawful and non-retaliatory, or that any specific landlord conduct involving immigration status was in fact retaliatory.

REMEDIES AND PENALTIES UNDER CIVIL CODE SECTION 1942.5
A landlord or a landlord's agent who violates this statute is liable to the tenant in a civil action for the tenant's actual damages, plus punitive damages of not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 for each retaliatory act, where the landlord or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that act. In an action brought for damages for retaliatory eviction, the court awards reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party if either party requests attorney's fees at the initiation of the action. These remedies are in addition to any other remedies provided by statutory or decisional law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any lessor or agent of a lessor who violates this section shall be liable to the lessee in a civil action for all of the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, civil liability for a violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "(2) Punitive damages in an amount of not less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than two thousand dollars ($2,000) for each retaliatory act where the lessor or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that act."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(h)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the punitive-damages figure and its fraud/oppression/malice condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "In any action brought for damages for retaliatory eviction, the court shall award reasonable attorney’s fees to the prevailing party if either party requests attorney’s fees upon the initiation of the action."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, attorney's fees to the prevailing party (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  "The remedies provided by this section shall be in addition to any other remedies provided by statutory or decisional law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1942.5(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, these remedies are cumulative with other remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1942.5.)
  Known gap: The punitive-damages range stated here — not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 per retaliatory act — is the statute's own current figure, verified against the actual fetched text rather than assumed; it applies only where the landlord or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that specific act, not to every violation of the statute. The attorney's-fee provision is not one-directional on its face: it states that the court awards fees "to the prevailing party," not only to a prevailing tenant, if either party requests fees when the action is initiated. This clause describes only the remedies the statute itself authorizes; the statute's text does not specify, and this document does not independently address, the procedural vehicle for bringing such an action (for example, as an affirmative civil suit versus as a defense or cross-complaint in an unlawful detainer proceeding), which is a different question from what remedies the statute makes available. All four citations below are subsections — (h) (in two parts) and (i) and (j) — of the same statutory section as this document's other Civil Code § 1942.5 clauses, not independently authored sources. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact substring of that fetched text. This is one state's statute; remedies for landlord retaliation, where recognized, vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not determine that any specific landlord violated this statute, that any specific conduct involved fraud, oppression, or malice, or that any specific tenant or landlord is entitled to any specific award.

SIGNATURE AND RECORD OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding the condition described above at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, rented by Jordan Lee from Pat Morgan, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice, does not itself exercise any right under Civil Code section 1942, and does not determine that any landlord conduct described in it was retaliatory under Civil Code section 1942.5.

Reporting, or threatening to report, the tenant or individuals known to the landlord to be associated with the tenant to immigration authorities is itself a form of retaliatory conduct the statute prohibits, and that specific prohibition does not limit the broader definition of retaliatory conduct the statute otherwise covers. The statute does not limit a landlord's lawful exercise of rights under a lease, agreement, or other law, or a landlord's right to take the described actions for any lawful cause, and any waiver by a tenant of rights under this statute is void as against public policy. Despite the 180-day rule, a landlord may still recover possession, increase rent, decrease services, or take the other described actions within that period if the notice of termination, rent increase, or other act — or a pleading or statement of issues in an arbitration — states the ground on which the landlord, in good faith, is acting; if the tenant disputes that stated ground, the landlord must establish its truth at the trial or other hearing.

expectedJSON.body: A landlord or a landlord's agent who violates this statute is liable to the tenant in a civil action for the tenant's actual damages, plus punitive damages of not less than $100 nor more than $2,000 for each retaliatory act, where the landlord or agent has been guilty of fraud, oppression, or malice with respect to that act. In an action brought for damages for retaliatory eviction, the court awards reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party if either party requests attorney's fees at the initiation of the action. These remedies are in addition to any other remedies provided by statutory or decisional law.
